method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope' (published 5 January 2023), 22 claims; LICENCE: © Springer Nature (exclusive rights under a publishing agreement; free to read, no open licence) (read at nature.com article page, 'Rights and permissions' section). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)' (2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version)), 5 claims; LICENCE: © European Association of Urology: personal and educational use only; no reproduction without written permission; AI-use clause (see method) (read at https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, chapter 10 'Copyright and terms of use'). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Source text: nature.com article HTML (full text returned without login), article body extracted with tags, tables and reference anchors stripped. Boxes 1 and 2 are in the text; Tables 1 and 2 were not extracted. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (2026 edition): the uroweb.org web chapter HTML, taken from the page data and tag-stripped, paraphrased and hash-anchored; the S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. EAU terms of use (chapter 10), verbatim: 'The content of the EAU Guidelines and all products derived from them is made available for personal and educational use only. No commercial usage is authorised. No part of the EAU Guidelines or any related products may be translated or reproduced in any form without written permission from the EAU. Furthermore, the EAU prohibits the usage or upload of its Guidelines, and any material derived from these texts (whether in full or in part) on external websites, bots, pages, portals, servers, software, or external applications, including those employing artificial intelligence technologies and infrastructure, such as large language models and generative AI, deep learning and machine learning, unless written permission has been granted for such by the EAU.' Under the owner's standing decision (Wave 4) an AI-use clause does not exclude a source; the clause is recorded here and S2 is paraphrased, not reproduced.

claims.claim: **PH is a group of recessive disorders that overproduce oxalate,** causing stones and nephrocalcinosis; more than 70% of patients reach kidney failure. Once GFR drops below 30–40 mL/min/1.73 m², oxalate builds up in bone, heart, vessels, nerves and eyes.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Type 1 is the commonest and most severe.** Infantile oxalosis (kidney failure before age 1) is the worst form; more than 50% of infants diagnosed with PH1 already have stage 5 CKD, often with poor feeding and failure to thrive. Manage them in highly specialised paediatric centres.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Everyone suspected of PH should have genetic testing,** the gold standard, because the type and genotype drive treatment. With eGFR under 30, get the result within 30 days.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **With eGFR above 30, measure urine oxalate at least twice** (a 24-hour collection is preferred, or a spot sample corrected for creatinine). Above 1 mmol/1.73 m² per day strongly suggests PH. Rule out enteric causes (for example pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, bowel disease, bariatric surgery) first.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **EAU urine oxalate bands (adults):** over 0.40 mmol a day confirms hyperoxaluria. Primary hyperoxaluria mostly exceeds 1 mmol a day; secondary (enteric or dietary) hyperoxaluria is usually between 0.5 and 1; 0.40–0.50 is the mild form common in idiopathic calcium oxalate stone formers.
claims.locator: European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel, 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)', 2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **In kidney failure, use plasma oxalate, not urine,** and compare results with dialysis patients who do not have PH rather than with healthy people. Plasma assays vary a lot between laboratories.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hydration is the cornerstone:** at least 2–3 L/m² body surface area a day in children (a gastrostomy may be needed in infants), and 3.5–4 L a day in adults per EAU advice.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Add citrate,** though the evidence is weak (one small study used 0.1–0.15 g/kg).
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A strict low-oxalate diet is not advised,** but limit very high-oxalate foods such as spinach, rhubarb, chocolate and nuts.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start pyridoxine (vitamin B6) in everyone with suspected PH or proven PH1,** up to 5 mg/kg (higher doses risk neurotoxicity). Responsiveness is a fall in urine oxalate of more than 30%, judged on at least two samples after at least 2 weeks; if responsive, taper to the lowest effective dose.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **EAU: pyridoxine for PH1 at 5–20 mg/kg a day,** set by the urine oxalate response and tolerance; its drug table gives a 5 mg/kg/day start, a 20 mg/kg/day maximum, and sensory peripheral neuropathy as the main risk. In about one-third of PH1 patients it normalises or markedly lowers urine oxalate.
claims.locator: European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel, 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)', 2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **EAU fluids and citrate:** adults 3.5–4.0 L a day and children 1.5 L/m2 of body surface, drunk on a round-the-clock schedule; alkaline citrate 3.25–9.75 g a day in adults (the children's dose is printed as 0.1–0.15 mg/kg a day; see Unresolved). Refer every patient to a specialised centre with an experienced interdisciplinary team.
claims.locator: European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel, 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)', 2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **RNAi therapy is indicated when genetics show pyridoxine-unresponsive PH1,** at any eGFR. Partial pyridoxine responders may qualify if hyperoxaluria persists (or, with eGFR under 30, depending on plasma oxalate).
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lumasiran silences glycolate oxidase.** In the Illuminate A trial (age over 6), urine oxalate fell by 65% versus 11% on placebo, and fifty-two per cent normalised. Children under 6 (Illuminate B) had a 72% fall in the oxalate-to-creatinine ratio. Side effects were minor injection-site reactions.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In reduced kidney function (Illuminate C, eGFR under 45),** plasma oxalate fell by an average of 42% in patients on dialysis.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor on RNAi therapy (eGFR above 30):** every 3–6 months in year one, then 6-monthly for 5 years, then yearly: urine oxalate, glycolate, citrate, calcium and creatinine, kidney function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, bone and heart imaging and an eye check. With eGFR under 30 or on dialysis, check plasma oxalate and bloods every 3 months.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Long-term effect on kidney outcomes is still unproven:** RNAi drugs clearly lower oxalate production, but longer data are needed on stones and kidney failure.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **EAU: prescribe lumasiran for PH type 1 that does not respond to pyridoxine** (strong; evidence level 1b that it lowers urine oxalate and stone recurrence). It may also stabilise GFR and improve nephrocalcinosis. Nedosiran was not yet EMA-approved when the EAU wrote this.
claims.locator: European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel, 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)', 2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Lumasiran dosing (EAU), by subcutaneous injection:** loading doses once a month for three months, 6 mg/kg below 10 kg and at 10–20 kg, and 3 mg/kg above 20 kg; maintenance from one month later, 3 mg/kg monthly below 10 kg, 6 mg/kg every three months at 10–20 kg, and 3 mg/kg every three months above 20 kg.
claims.locator: European Association of Urology (EAU) Urolithiasis Guidelines Panel, 'EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis (section 4.6.3, Primary hyperoxaluria, and the drug table)', 2026 edition (full update of the 2025 publication; web version), https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Consider dialysis early in stage 4–5 CKD,** before uraemia, when plasma oxalate stays high despite treatment or there are signs of systemic oxalosis. Standard dialysis removes far less oxalate than PH1 produces.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prefer intensive haemodialysis over peritoneal dialysis** (high-flux, maximal blood flow, daily if tolerated, with more sessions rather than longer ones), aiming for pre-dialysis plasma oxalate of about 50–70 μmol/L. Watch phosphate closely.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Liver transplant is the only cure for PH1;** remove the native liver (auxiliary grafts are obsolete). In kidney failure, combined liver–kidney transplant gives much better kidney-graft survival than kidney alone (87% versus 14% at 15 years). Kidney-only transplant is an option for pyridoxine responders who normalise urine oxalate.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Skipping liver transplant on lumasiran is a careful, case-by-case decision** with intensive monitoring. Lumasiran does not clear oxalate already stored in the body, so after a kidney-only graft keep up hyperhydration and alkalinisation.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For stone removal, percutaneous nephrolithotomy has worked best in PH1;** shock-wave lithotripsy gives poor stone-free rates. Otherwise follow EAU stone algorithms.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Keep patients hyperhydrated throughout any operation and avoid pre-operative fluid fasting:** even mild dehydration can cause acute kidney injury.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Never discharge from follow-up.** Image the kidneys 6-monthly for 2 years, then at least yearly; ultrasound at least yearly before stage 5D, avoiding radiation where possible.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Routine checks on conventional therapy:** urine oxalate and creatinine every 3–12 months (plasma oxalate only in CKD 4 or worse), growth, bone chemistry, thyroid and vitamin D yearly, and yearly eye and heart checks when eGFR is under 30 or on dialysis.
claims.locator: ERKNet and OxalEurope (Groothoff JW et al.), Nature Reviews Nephrology, 'Clinical practice recommendations for primary hyperoxaluria: an expert consensus statement from ERKNet and OxalEurope', published 5 January 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-022-00661-1, retrieved 2026-09-23
